name: Tinted eye cream

lead: A tinted eye cream is an eye moisturizer with a light pigment, so it hides under-eye discoloration while hydrating, in one step instead of a separate concealer. The fresher, brighter look is immediate.

The tint, often iron oxides or similar pigments, optically masks darker or bluish skin. Added ingredients such as caffeine, peptides, hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide or mineral sunscreen are described as acting in other ways, such as constricting vessels, brightening or hydrating. Studies behind those longer-term claims generally tested untinted eye creams and serums.

paras: People pat it under the eyes in the morning in place of eye cream and light concealer, sometimes with a concealer on top for more cover. The cover washes off at night; any skincare benefit from the actives builds with regular use.

Reported risks include allergic contact dermatitis of the eyelids, including to iron oxide pigments, irritation from some preservatives, product migrating into the eye, and milia with heavy occlusive bases. Cosmetics are generally sold without prescription.

angle.text: Users apply a tinted eye cream to conceal dark circles while moisturizing in a single step, and the cover is visible immediately. Studies of the active ingredients, such as caffeine, have generally used untinted eye products.

lead: A tinted eye cream is a cosmetic that combines a sheer pigment with the moisturizing and active ingredients of a conventional eye cream, made for the thin skin under the eyes. People use it to make dark circles and under-eye discoloration look less visible while hydrating, in one step instead of applying a separate concealer.[1]

Typical formulas are described as including mineral sunscreens such as zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, antioxidants, peptides, caffeine and hyaluronic acid.[1] Dark circles have several recognised causes, grouped by Wikipedia into structural (thin skin, bone and muscle shape, volume loss), vascular (venous congestion, visible veins in pale skin) and pigmented (extra melanin from sun or rubbing) types.[2]

The immediate camouflage is the effect of the tint. Wikipedia lists caffeine as a vasoconstrictor and vitamin C as a possible brightener among topical agents used for dark circles, and studies cited in popular reference material generally tested untinted eye creams or serums.[1][2]
infobox: Pigments (often iron oxides), caffeine, peptides, hyaluronic acid, antioxidants, mineral SPF[1]
Immediate camouflage; other claimed benefits less studied

paras: The product sits between a tinted moisturizer and a concealer, with lighter coverage than most concealers and the hydration of an eye cream. Some versions include SPF for daily use.[1]

Described active ingredients include caffeine (said to narrow small vessels and reduce the look of puffiness), vitamin C and niacinamide (brightening), peptides (fine lines) and hyaluronic acid (hydration).[1] Wikipedia also describes caffeine as a vasoconstrictor and vitamin C as a brightener in creams marketed for dark circles.[2]

Reference material traces the format to the broader move toward hybrid skincare-makeup products, including tinted moisturizers in the 1990s and 2000s and BB and CC creams from Korean brands, with eye-specific tinted products becoming more visible in the 2010s and on social media from around 2020.[1] That account comes from an AI-generated encyclopedia entry, and some of its supporting citations are commercial pages, so specific dates are uncertain.

Concealment is immediate and depends on shade match and undertone. Longer-term claims draw on studies of eye creams generally, for example reported reductions in dark-circle appearance over weeks with caffeine- or vitamin-containing products.[1] Those studies were not of tinted products specifically.[1]

Because dark circles are multifactorial, a product that addresses pigment, visible vessels or shadowing from anatomy may work differently across people.[2] Dermatology blogs and brands also describe iron oxide pigments as adding coverage and some protection against visible light; these are brand and practitioner claims rather than independent trials.

Reported problems include allergic contact dermatitis on the eyelids, including to iron oxide pigments; irritation from preservatives such as methylisothiazolinone; product migrating into the eyes; and milia associated with heavy, occlusive bases.[1] Product-use guidance in the same source suggests patch testing and that people with rosacea or who are pregnant consult a dermatologist.[1]
The product is discussed in grooming contexts as a low-effort way to reduce the appearance of tired eyes, combining cover and treatment claims.
No studies found. Studies of untinted eye creams and serums exist, but none identified test a tinted eye cream as such.[1]
